newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK RATES DAZZLED BY CBANK MOVE SEEK EQUILIBRIUM.
newsitem.headline: GREEK RATES DAZZLED BY CBANK MOVE SEEK EQUILIBRIUM.

text.p: Greek depos and forex forwards were gyrating seeking equilibrium a day after the central bank announced new ways of conducting money market operations and dealers said state securities stood to gain the most from the move.

"Rates have been volatile and the market is nervous trying to adjust to the new situation," said a dealer at a foreign bank. "The central bank's move is going to drain some liquidity from the market by redirecting it into government T-bills and bonds."

Implied forward drachma rates from forex swaps were fluctuating in the 6.0 to 9.0 percent band from tomnext to one-week, 9.40-9.90 percent from one-week to two-months and 10.20-10.30 percent from six-months to one-year, dealers said.
"I have never seen such a thing," said a trader at a foreign bank. "I think it is going to take about a week for the market to calm down."
Bank of Greece announced on Wednesday that it would hold regular, weekly 14-day depo and repo tenders in an effort to fine tune liquidity and harmonise operations with those expected under EMU.
It will also set up a facility accepting depos up to 300 billion drachmas from the market at 11.90 percent and amounts over it at 9.9 percent from March 28.
Bank of Greece used to intervene to drain huge amounts of money daily, estimates put it between 1.0 and 1.4 trillion drachmas lately, in the last few months.

Central bank governor Lucas Papademos told reporters on Wednesday that the cost of these interventions was some 40 billion drachmas in 1996. The central bank posted pretax profits of 36.6 billion drachmas in 1996, up 5.0 percent on 1995.

Commercial banks have engaged in profitable arbitrage against the central bank in the last few months by borrowing drachmas through forex swaps at rates below 11 percent and placing them with the central bank at 11.90 percent, dealers said.
"There is still room for this type of arbitrage although it is riskier but I expect the dominant feature of the market in the next few days to be credit limit arbitrage between banks," he said.

Some commercial banks were unable to place their drachmas with other banks offering attractive interest rates today because of their credit limits and were forced to deposit them with others at much lower interest rates creating confusion in the process, traders said.

The central bank has made no secret of its desire to chase away the speculative forex component of the excess interbank liquidity and purge likely inflationary pressures in the medium-term by pre-emptying them.
M3 money supply grew 13.8 percent year-on-year in January overshooting the central bank's target of 6.0-9.0 percent for end-97.
However some bankers pointed out that the main cause of excess liquidity was the budget financing policy pursued by the state.

"The finance ministry has been pursuing an aggressive policy of interest rate cuts in the last few months supported by the reduction of its cash reserves at the central bank which flooded the market with money in the process," said a senior banker at a foreign bank.

Yannis Stournaras, chairman of the council of economic advisors at the national economy ministry, told daily Kerdos recently that cash reserves should not exceed 300 billion drachmas at any point in time.
The finance ministry has managed to bring cash reserves down to about 800 billion drachmas recently from 1.2 trillion in the past, said Stournaras.

Other bankers said cheaper foreign currency denominated loans taken by local corporations were also responsible for the burgeoning liquidity. Press reports have said forex loans accounted for about one third of all loans at end-1996.
Th finance ministry is going to apply the Law 128 contribution of 1.0 percent to all loans irrespective of their interest rate levels, sources said.
Currently, loans carrying rates up to 5.0 percent are exempted from the 1.0 percent contribution.

"Bank of Greece opted for a shock therapy instead of a gradual treatment of the problem of excess liquidity," said a senior trader at a foreign bank. "It will not take long to determine whether these policy measures are effective." -- Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
